title: The Chafetz Chaim (Psalm 34:13–14)
hook: Israel Meir Kagan's book on speech takes its name from "Who is the man that desireth life"

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lashon hara, and your line: no gossip. Today, the book that gathered the rules for it.

A peddler is walking through the towns of Galilee, calling out like any street seller: who wants to buy the elixir of life? A rabbi named Yannai, studying nearby, hears him and calls him over. The peddler doesn't open a bottle. He opens a book of Psalms and points to a verse. That's the story the midrash tells. The verse would one day name a book, and the book would name the man who wrote it.
screen: `WHO WANTS THE ELIXIR OF LIFE?` → `HE OPENS THE PSALMS.` → `A VERSE BECOMES A NAME.`

segments.voice: The Chafetz Chaim. In Hebrew, chafetz chaim means desiring life. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. Psalm thirty-four, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, asks: "Who is the man that desireth life, and loveth days, that he may see good therein?" A question with a lot of hands going up. Then the answer: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." Not a diet. Not a medicine. The tongue. Second, the book. A rabbi named Israel Meir Kagan, living among the Jews of Eastern Europe, wrote a book gathering the laws of guarding speech: what counts as lashon hara, when speaking is forbidden, when it's required to protect someone. He named it from this verse: Chafetz Chaim. Third, the man who became his book. People came to call the author by its title, and the name stuck. An unusual kind of fame, being named for a book about what not to say. Fourth, the next verse. The psalm doesn't stop at keeping quiet: depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it. Guarding the tongue isn't only a fence. It makes room for peace. Yesterday named the harm; today hands it a discipline, with a verse at the front. And the question still stands open: who wants life?
screen: `WHO IS THE MAN THAT DESIRETH LIFE?` · `A BOOK OF THE LAWS OF SPEECH.` · `THE MAN BECAME HIS BOOK.` · `SEEK PEACE, AND PURSUE IT.` · then, large: `KEEP THY TONGUE FROM EVIL.`

segments.voice: Touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your teeth and feel how small it is, and how much it does. Run through the day ahead, pick one conversation that could easily tilt, and decide now what you'll do if a story starts: let it pass, or turn it toward something good. If you pray, say the psalm's line, keep thy tongue from evil; if not, hold the question, who wants life?
The Chafetz Chaim. Desiring life: the psalm's question, the title of Israel Meir Kagan's book on guarding speech, and the name people gave the man. Today's word.
Your line: keep thy tongue from evil. The psalm goes on: seek peace, and pursue it. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jews study a short section of the Chafetz Chaim's laws of speech each day, often in study groups or with a daily calendar, and Psalm 34's verses on the tongue are sung in some prayer services.

It was his family name, passed down through many generations of his ancestors.
The peddler in the midrash gave him that nickname when they met in Galilee.
